title: The Lady, or the Tiger?
focus: a choice the reader must make

teacherSummary.text: A semi-barbaric king judges the accused in an arena: the accused opens one of two doors, behind one a tiger, behind the other a lady he must marry. When the princess's lowborn lover is caught, she learns which door hides which. She signals him to the right-hand door. The story ends without telling us what came out.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Lady, or the Tiger?,” how does Stockton show a choice the reader must make? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the structure you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Lady, or the Tiger?, how does Stockton develop the idea of a choice the reader must make? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the structure in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Lady, or the Tiger? develops the idea of a choice the reader must make. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Lady, or the Tiger? (where it begins, turns and ends) and its structure shape the reader's understanding of a choice the reader must make. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Lady, or the Tiger? suggests about a choice the reader must make. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's structure and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Frank R. Stockton uses structure in The Lady, or the Tiger? to complicate the reader's understanding of a choice the reader must make. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Lady, or the Tiger? within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of a choice the reader must make responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Lady, or the Tiger? alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of a choice the reader must make follows or bends those conventions, using the structure as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Lady, or the Tiger? and its treatment of a choice the reader must make. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's structure and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Lady, or the Tiger? as evidence for a larger claim about a choice the reader must make in The Lady, or the Tiger?. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Lady, or the Tiger? as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of a choice the reader must make. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Lady, or the Tiger?.

Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Stockton's description of the princess gives evidence for both endings. When the text says “She raised her hand, and made a slight, quick movement toward the right” (The Lady, or the Tiger?, paragraph 17), it shows this directly. She shares her father's "semi-barbaric" nature and has thought jealously about the lady, yet she loves the man; when she makes "a slight, quick movement toward the right," the reader must decide which side of her won.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Implied violent death. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes implied violent death.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”
